# Introduction

In this assignment, you will practice regression analysis including:

-   Plotting bivariate data with a regression line
-   Calculating and interpreting the correlation coefficient, r
-   Fitting a linear regression analysis
-   Verifying if a linear model is model is adequate:
    -   Checking for linearity (scatterplot)
    -   Checking for constant variance (`plot(lm_output, which=1)`)
    -   Checking for normality of residuals (`qqPlot(lm_output$residuals)`)

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(rio)
library(car)

```

# Car Prices and Mileage

<p align="center">

<img src="https://github.com/byuistats/Math221D_Cannon/raw/master/Images/Accura_MDX.png" width="310" height="200"/>

</p>

You are interested in purchasing an all wheel drive Acura MDX for those slick Rexburg winters. You found what you think is a good deal for on a low-mileage 2020 model but you'd like to be sure. You go on Autotrader.com and randomly select 23 Acura MDX's and collect Price and Mileage information.

Load the data and use R to answer the questions below.

```{r}

cars <- import('https://github.com/byuistats/Math221D_Cannon/raw/master/Data/acuraMDX_price_vs_mileage.csv')

view(cars)
```

Before you begin:

**What is the response/dependent variable?**

Price

**What is the explanatory variable**

Milage

**What do you think is the nature of the relationship between the two?**

Negative

**How strong do you think the relationship is?**

Fairly strong

## Plot the Data and calculate r

```{r}
ggplot(cars, aes(x = Mileage, y = `MDX Price`)) +
  geom_point(color = '2') +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Mileage and Price") 

cor(`MDX Price` ~ Mileage, data = cars)

```

**Does the relationship look linear?**

yes

**What is the correlation coefficient, r?**

-0.8185192

**What does this r show?**

Negative and strong linear relationship

## Fit a Linear Regression Model

```{r}

car.lm <- lm(`MDX Price` ~ Mileage, data = cars)
summary(car.lm)

```

Add the regression line to your chart:

```{r}
# Sometimes you have to run the whole chunk with plot() and the abline() together:

#plot()
#abline(lm_output$coefficients)

ggplot(cars, aes(x = Mileage, y = `MDX Price`)) +
  geom_point(color = '2') +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Mileage and Price") +
  geom_smooth(method="lm")

```

**What is the slope of the regression line, and what does it mean?**

For every mile the price goes down 5 cents

**What is the intercept and what does it mean?**

when mileage is 0 the price is 17930

**What is your p-value?**

1.81e-06

**What is your conclusion?**

We can reject the null because the p-value is less than the level of significance. We can conclude that the true population slope is != 0 meaning that there is a significant linear relationship between mileage and price.

**What is the confidence interval for the slope?**

```         
6.659524e-02 -3.442092e-02
```

```{r}
confint(car.lm, level = 0.95)
```

Interpret the confidence interval.

We are 95% sure that the true regression slope is between -0.065 and -0.0344. Since 0 is not in the interval we have a significant slope.

## Check Model Requirements

Check the normality of the residuals:

It looks pretty normal

```{r}
qqPlot(car.lm$residuals)
```

Check for constant variance (Residual by Predicted plot):

```{r}
plot(car.lm, which = 1)
```

We have constant variance

Lastly, the car you're interested in buying has around 100,000 miles and costs \$11,200. Could this be considered a good deal? Why?

This car is a good deal because the expected price is higher than the offer that we got.

# Manatee Deaths and Motorboat Registrations in Florida

<p align="center">

<img src="https://github.com/byuistats/Math221D_Cannon/raw/master/Images/manatees1.png" width="300" height="300"/>

</p>

Florida is a fabulous place for experiencing wildlife and recreation. Unfortunately, sometimes those two activities conflict.

Researchers collected over 30 years of data about water craft registrations (motor and non-motor boats) and manatee deaths. The goal of the research is to evaluate the relationship between boat registrations and manatee deaths.

Before you begin:

**What is the response/dependent variable?**

Manatee deaths

**What is the explanatory variable**

Boat registrations

**What do you think is the nature of the relationship between the two?**

Positive

**How strong do you think the relationship is?**

Strong

Load the data:

```{r}
manatees <- import('https://github.com/byuistats/Math221D_Cannon/raw/master/Data/manatees.csv')
view(manatees)
```

## Plot the Data and calculate r

```{r}
ggplot(manatees, aes(x = `Power Boats (in 1000's)`, y = Manatees)) +
  geom_point(color = '2') +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Mileage and Price") 

cor(Manatees ~ `Power Boats (in 1000's)`, data = manatees)

```

**Does the relationship look linear?**

yes

**What is the correlation coefficient, r?**

0.9376368

**What does this r show?**

R shows that it is a strong positive linear relationship since the max it can be is 1.

## Fit a Linear Regression Model

```{r}
manatee.lm <- lm(Manatees ~ `Power Boats (in 1000's)`, data = manatees)
summary(manatee.lm)

```

Add the regression line to your chart:

```{r}
# Sometimes you have to do the plot() and the abline() in one chunk and run the whole thing:
ggplot(manatees, aes(x = `Power Boats (in 1000's)`, y = Manatees)) +
  geom_point(color = '2') +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Boat Registration and Manatee Deaths") +
  geom_smooth(method="lm")

```

**What is the slope of the regression line, and what does it mean?**

The slope is 6.8 meaning that for every boat in the water, 7 manatees die.

**What is the intercept and what does it mean?**

The intercept means that on their own, the population would grow by 42 manatees a year

**What is your p-value?**

1.25e-07

**What is your conclusion?**

We reject the null hypothesis because our p-value is below the level of significance. The true population slope is not = 0 meaning that there is a significant linear relationship between boat registrations and manatee deaths.

**What is the confidence interval for the slope?**

```{r}
confint(manatee.lm, level = 0.95)
```

**Interpret the confidence interval:** We are 95% sure that the true regression slope lies between 0.1121773 and 0.1460879

Check the normality of the residuals:

```{r}
qqPlot(manatee.lm$residuals)
```

Check for constant variance (Residual by Predicted plot):

We do not have constant variance

```{r}

plot(manatee.lm, which = 1)
```

# MCAT Score and GPA

<p align="center">

<img src="https://github.com/byuistats/Math221D_Cannon/raw/master/Images/MCAT_official_logo.png" width="300" height="200"/>

</p>

The MCAT is an entrance exam for medical schools. It seems likely that there is a relationship between your undergraduate GPA and how well you do on the MCAT.

GPA and MCAT score data were collected on 55 prospective medical students.

Before you begin:

**What is the response/dependent variable?**

MCAT Score

**What is the explanatory variable**

GPA

**What do you think is the nature of the relationship between the two?**

As GPA increases the probably of a high MCAT score goes up

**How strong do you think the relationship is?**

Positive and stronger than 0

Load the data:

```{r}
mcat <- import('https://github.com/byuistats/Math221D_Cannon/raw/master/Data/mcat_gpa.csv')

```

## Plot the Data and calculate r

```{r}
ggplot(mcat, aes(x = GPA, y = MCAT)) +
  geom_point(color = '2') +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs( 
    title = "MCAT score and GPA") 

cor(MCAT ~ GPA, data = mcat)

```

**Does the relationship look linear?**

Yes

**What is the correlation coefficient, r?**

0.5414202

**What does this r show?**

This shows a positive and strong linear relationship.

## Fit a Linear Regression Model

```{r}
mcat.lm <- lm(MCAT ~ GPA, data = mcat)
summary(mcat.lm)

```

Add the regression line to your chart:

```{r}
# Sometimes you have to do the plot() and the abline() in one chunk and run the whole thing:
ggplot(mcat, aes(x = GPA, y = MCAT)) +
  geom_point(color = '2') +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs( 
    title = "MCAT scores and GPA") +
  geom_smooth(method="lm")

```

**What is the slope of the regression line, and what does it mean?**

Slope is 9 so for every point up in GPA, you get 9 more points on the MCAT

**What is the intercept and what does it mean?**

The intercept it 3.9 so at a gpa of 0 you will get a score of 3.9

**What is your p-value?**

The p-value is 0.573

**What is your conclusion?**

We fail to reject the null hypothesis because the p-value is higher than the level of significance. The true population slope is not = 0 meaning that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that there is a significant linear relationship between GPA and MCAT scores.

**What is the confidence interval for the slope?**

```{r}
confint(mcat.lm, level = 0.95)
```

**Interpret the confidence interval:**

We are 95% certain that the true population slope lies between 5.209161 and 12.99928. Since 0 is not in the interval we have a significant slope

## Check Model Requirements

Check the normality of the residuals:

```{r}
qqPlot(mcat.lm$residuals)
```

Check for constant variance (Residual by Predicted plot):

```{r}

plot(mcat.lm, which = 1)
```

We have normal variance
